The majority voted in favour of a [motion](http://www.openaustralia.org/debate/?id=2014-03-24.136.8) that the bill be agreed to, which ends the consideration and detail stage.(Read more about the stages that a bill must pass through to become law [here](http://www.peo.gov.au/learning/fact-sheets/making-a-law.html). ) That the House of Representatives can now decide on whether to read the bill a third time and therefore pass it in the House. _Background to the bill_ In the [2013 election](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_federal_election,_2013) campaign, the [Coalition](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coalition_%28Australia%29) said that it would be an infrastructure-focused government and committed to finding ways to encourage the private sector to become more involved in infrastructure financing. This bill reflects that commitment by amending the _Nation Building Program (National Land Transport) Act 2009_ ('the Act') to allow partnerships and non-corporate Commonwealth entities, such as public private partnerships, to be funded. The bill also renames the Act to the _National Land Transport Act 2014_ and continues the [Roads to Recovery Programme](http://investment.infrastructure.gov.au/funding/r2r/) after 30 June 2014, when it is currently scheduled to end.(Read more about the bill in the [bills digest](http://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd1314a/14bd091).)

The majority voted in favour of a [motion](http://www.openaustralia.org/senate/?gid=2014-08-28.7.23) that the bill be read a second time.(Read more about the stages that a bill must pass through to become law [here](http://www.peo.gov.au/learning/fact-sheets/making-a-law.html). ) This means that the majority agree with the main idea of the bill and that the Senate can now consider the bill in more detail. _Background to the bill_ In the [2013 election](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_federal_election,_2013) campaign, the [Coalition](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coalition_%28Australia%29) said that it would be an infrastructure-focused government and committed to finding ways to encourage the private sector to become more involved in infrastructure financing. This bill reflects that commitment by amending the _Nation Building Program (National Land Transport) Act 2009_ ('the Act') to allow partnerships and non-corporate Commonwealth entities, such as public private partnerships, to be funded. The bill also renames the Act to the _National Land Transport Act 2014_ and continues the [Roads to Recovery Programme](http://investment.infrastructure.gov.au/funding/r2r/) after 30 June 2014, when it is currently scheduled to end.(Read more about the bill in the [bills digest](http://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd1314a/14bd091).)

Moved the second reading of the Land Transport Infrastructure Amendment Bill 2014, which renames the National Land Transport Act, continues the Roads to Recovery program beyond 30 June 2014, and gives effect to the government's $35.5 billion, six-year Infrastructure Investment Program, including a $6.7 billion Bruce Highway upgrade.

Argued that Labor's infrastructure legacy, including doubling the roads budget to $46.5 billion and rebuilding or upgrading 7,500 kilometres of road and nearly 4,000 kilometres of rail, took Australia from 20th to first among OECD countries for infrastructure investment as a share of GDP between 2007 and 2013.

Supported the Land Transport Infrastructure Amendment Bill, said the government has committed $35 billion to road and rail projects including $1.5 billion for Melbourne's East West Link, expected to create 3,200 jobs and deliver $1.40 in benefits per dollar spent, and noted protester Anthony Maine boasted his activities had cost police more than $2 million.

Explained the bill continues the Roads to Recovery program beyond 30 June 2014, citing the government's $35.5 billion Infrastructure Investment Program over six years, noted $1.75 billion had been provided under Roads to Recovery from 2009-10 to 2013-14, including $373.5 million in 2013-14 alone, and said more than $40 million had gone to Brisbane City Council.

Criticised the bill for omitting any funding for urban rail, noting Infrastructure Australia assessed the Melbourne Metro rail tunnel as ready to proceed in 2012 and Labor had pledged $3 billion toward it, and contrasted this with the Prime Minister's unassessed East West Link, which former Infrastructure Australia head Michael Deegan said would return just 80 cents for every dollar spent.

Highlighted the $6.7 billion Bruce Highway upgrade as the biggest single commitment under the government's infrastructure program, citing 170 deaths and 1,620 hospitalisations on the highway between 2008 and 2011. Welcomed the five-year extension of the Roads to Recovery program with $1.75 billion in funding.

Backed the bill's continuation of the Roads to Recovery program, detailing its impact across the eight councils in her Indi electorate. Noted Alpine Shire alone has received $2,806,434 in funding since 2009, supporting road and bridge maintenance across a network of hundreds of kilometres in each local government area.

Welcomed a further $1.75 billion to extend the Roads to Recovery program for five years, and highlighted the $3 billion NorthConnex project, which will receive $405 million from the federal government. Criticised Labor's handling of the Tourle Street bridge, saying building it with only two lanes instead of four will now cost an extra $100 million rather than the original $15 million.

Backed the bill's extension of road funding, recalling that as a candidate in 1995 he visited the Hunter Expressway site with then Minister for Roads Laurie Brereton to confirm Labor's commitment to the project.

Backed continuation of the Roads to Recovery program, noting four councils in his Lyne electorate have shared more than $42 million in funding since it began. Contrasted this with Sydney City Council spending $110,000 on a rainbow-coloured pedestrian crossing and then $30,000 to remove it, while one regional council must maintain 1,200 kilometres of unsealed road and 72 bridges.

Opposed the Moorebank intermodal project as a multibillion dollar mistake, warning the only rail line serving it, the Southern Sydney Freight Line, has a maximum capacity of about 1.9 million containers. Said the project would add 20,000 extra trucks a day near Liverpool Hospital, and argued a growing western Sydney population, projected to reach nearly 2,000,000 by 2030, made Moorebank the wrong location.

Criticised the government for re-announcing a $90 million package for six remote Northern Territory roads that Labor had already committed in 2012, accusing it of taking credit for existing investments. Cited a 250 per cent increase in infrastructure spending under Labor, from $1.6 billion to $4.12 billion, and warned that the closure of the Gove refinery would cost 1,200 jobs.

Highlighted $686 million for the Gateway WA project and $615 million for the Swan Valley Bypass under the government's national infrastructure investment program. Detailed Roads to Recovery projects in his Canning electorate, including a new road connecting Mandurah's train station to the city centre, and noted Boddington's Newmont goldmine produces about 800,000 ounces of gold a year.

Supported the bill's continuation of the Roads to Recovery program, and quoted the minister's own second reading speech committing $35.5 billion over six years to road and rail projects, including $6.7 billion to upgrade the Bruce Highway and $5.6 billion to finish duplicating the Pacific Highway, projects he said were conceived and begun under the previous Labor government.

Defended the bill, saying the government's $6.7 billion commitment to the Bruce Highway was $2.6 billion more than Labor had allocated, bringing total investment with Queensland government funding to $8.5 billion, and cited World Health Organization data ranking the Bruce Highway among the world's 22 worst roads due to its death toll.

Continued opposing the East West Link, citing former Infrastructure Australia head Michael Deegan's evidence that an alternative business case showed a benefit-cost ratio of just 0.8, meaning 80 cents returned for every dollar spent, and said the Prime Minister had pledged $1.5 billion toward the project despite forecasts of worsening congestion, with traffic expected to reach 80,000 vehicles a day when it opens in 2019.

Raised a point of order arguing the discussion of 457 visas was not relevant to the Land Transport Infrastructure Amendment Bill 2014, and asked the Deputy Speaker to bring the member back to the bill.

Supported the bill, citing the government's $1.5 billion commitment to the WestConnex project, which will let commuters bypass 52 sets of traffic lights and save 40 minutes, its $405 million contribution to the $3 billion NorthConnex project creating around 2,000 jobs, and a further $1.75 billion committed to extend Roads to Recovery for five more years.

Criticised the coalition for slashing $2 billion from the federal roads budget when previously in government, and listed Labor-funded projects including $686 million to finish the Gateway WA project in Perth and $400 million to continue the Midland Highway upgrade in Tasmania.

Defended the coalition's infrastructure record, citing $123 billion in accumulated deficits and $660 billion in projected debt under the previous Labor government as reasons voters removed it from office, and praised the Roads to Recovery program, established under the Howard government in 2005, for surviving changes of government.

Criticised the Land Transport Infrastructure Amendment Bill for shifting decision-making power from the independent Infrastructure Australia to the minister, said a cost-benefit analysis found the government's preferred South Road Darlington project returns just 66 cents per dollar spent versus $2.40 for an alternative widening project, and said South Australia has 11 per cent of the nation's roads but receives only about five per cent of federal road funding.

Supported the Land Transport Infrastructure Amendment Bill, said the government's $35.5 billion infrastructure package includes $1.75 billion to extend the Roads to Recovery program for another five years, and said his O'Connor electorate's 43 local councils received a combined $18,952,000 under the program in 2013 to 2014.

Supported the Land Transport Infrastructure Amendment Bill, said $300 million will fund planning for the inland rail line connecting Melbourne to Brisbane via Parkes in his Calare electorate, and said the Roads to Recovery program is worth $8 million to Calare councils, while a proposed Needles dam still needs $3 million to proceed.

Opposed the Land Transport Infrastructure Amendment Bill for ignoring public transport, said Melbourne's East West Link would take $1.5 billion from the foreign aid budget while returning just 80 cents for every dollar spent according to its business case, and said a single train to Doncaster could take 800 cars off the road.
